items.title: PyTorch 2.15 rebuilds distributed training — rewritten NCCL backend is now the default with legacy fallback, new flight recorder dumps on hangs, one-sided transport API lands with NIXL; CUDA 12.6 wheels dropped (Maxwell/Pascal/Volta), Python 3.10 support removed
items.summary: PyTorch 2.15 shipped on October 28, 2026. The release rewrites the NCCL process-group backend and makes the new implementation the default for every job using the `nccl` backend; the previous code remains available as `nccl-legacy` for rollback, selectable via `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0`, and is scheduled for removal in PyTorch 2.16 (planned for early 2027). The rewrite targets the classic distributed-training failure mode where a single malfunctioning GPU can hang an entire cluster, and ships with a backend-agnostic flight recorder that dumps per-rank state when a collective operation hangs — the same capability that in 2.14 required opt-in is now part of the default install. 2.15 also adds a `torch.distributed.transport` Python API for one-sided data movement (one rank reads from or writes to a remote buffer without the remote rank issuing a matching call), with an NVIDIA NIXL backend as the first implementation and CUDA-graph-capturable transfers. Compatibility caveats are significant: checkpoints saved by 2.15 cannot be loaded by 2.14 or earlier; CUDA 12.6 wheels are no longer published, dropping Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta GPU support; Python 3.10 wheels are also gone (2.14 was the last release to ship them); and the new NCCL backend expects NCCL 2.29+ and RCCL 2.30.7. The devclass write-up published November 7 is the clearest post-release independent coverage of the 'one bad GPU' framing.
items.why_it_matters: PyTorch 2.15 is the most consequential developer-tool release this half of November for anyone who touches ML training code, and it was missed by every prior digest/enrichment/refresh run in the last three weeks — worth catching up on now. Four threads worth noticing. First, the NCCL-backend rewrite is the biggest reliability improvement to multi-GPU training in PyTorch's history. The 'one bad GPU hangs the whole cluster' problem has cost frontier labs enormous amounts of wall-clock time for years — a single H100 going silent used to mean a full restart of a 1,000-GPU run. The new backend, combined with the always-on flight recorder, means diagnostics now dump automatically and debugging a hang goes from hours-of-log-grep to a structured per-rank snapshot. For anyone running even two-GPU training on a hobby setup, this matters: distributed training from a laptop + external GPU, or from Colab + a rented second node, becomes meaningfully more debuggable. Second, the hardware-compatibility break is sharp. CUDA 12.6 wheels are gone, which means PyTorch 2.15 will not install cleanly on consumer cards older than roughly 2020 (Maxwell/Pascal/Volta — think GTX 10-series, Titan V). If Gabe's local GPU is a GTX 1660 or older, upgrading to 2.15 means downgrading to 2.14 LTS or buying newer hardware. This is the first time PyTorch has dropped consumer-GPU wheels at a .15 minor release rather than at a major-version bump, and it is a signal that the framework's maintainers now consider pre-Ampere GPUs effectively legacy. Third, Python 3.10 support is removed — 2.14 is the last release with 3.10 wheels. If any dependency (older torch-adjacent packages, some scientific computing libraries, some hobby codebases) is pinned to Python 3.10, upgrading PyTorch now forces a Python upgrade first. On the Python-hobbyist side this is a nudge toward Python 3.12 or 3.13 as the practical default. Fourth, the one-sided transport API with the NIXL backend is the sleeper feature. One-sided reads and writes between ranks — without matching sends and receives — is how RDMA networking has worked for decades, but PyTorch is the first major ML framework to expose it as a first-class Python API. The practical consequence shows up first in inference serving: weight-sharing across model instances, parameter-server architectures, and serving stacks like vLLM and SGLang can now avoid a lot of synchronization overhead. For hobby inference the direct impact is small today, but the plumbing is now in place for genuinely novel serving architectures over the next year. Practical steps: if you have working PyTorch 2.14 code and are not training across GPUs, there is no rush. If you are doing any multi-GPU work, upgrade and set `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0` as your rollback escape hatch while you confirm the new default works. If you depend on CUDA 12.6 or Python 3.10, stay on 2.14 until you can migrate.
items.why_it_matters_brief: The rewritten NCCL backend is now the default and the flight recorder dumps on hangs — the 'one bad GPU hangs the whole cluster' problem is finally structurally addressed, at the cost of CUDA 12.6 and Python 3.10 wheels.

source.name: DevClass (primary post-release independent coverage — 'PyTorch 2.15 tackles the one bad GPU problem', Nov 7); PyTorch official release blog Oct 28 (primary release notes, not directly fetched); AlphaSignal ('PyTorch 2.15 Rebuilds Distributed Training and Cuts Decoding Overhead'); PyTorch Korean user group (release announcement with NCCL default behavior detail); PyTorch dev-discuss (CUDA 12.6 wheels notice; Python 3.10 removal notice); PyTorch docs (torch.distributed.transport one-sided API); FuturumGroup ('PyTorch 2.15: Open-Source AI's Production Inflection Point'); Welcome.ai (enterprise reliability framing); CryptoBriefing (NCCL backend + GPU recovery summary)

takes.source: DevClass — 'PyTorch 2.15 tackles the "one bad GPU" problem'
takes.take: Primary post-release independent coverage. Clearest framing of the NCCL-backend rewrite as a response to the single-GPU-hangs-the-cluster failure mode.

takes.source: AlphaSignal — 'PyTorch 2.15 Rebuilds Distributed Training and Cuts Decoding Overhead'
takes.take: Good complement to the DevClass piece. Summarizes the NCCL rewrite, the flight recorder, and the compatibility break on 2.14 checkpoints.

takes.source: PyTorch Korean user group — 'PyTorch 2.15 release notice'
takes.take: Clearest statement of the default-backend behavior: every job that uses `nccl` runs on the rewritten backend by default; `nccl-legacy` and `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0` as rollback paths.

takes.source: PyTorch dev-discuss — 'CUDA 12.6 wheels will no longer be published from PyTorch 2.15 (drops Maxwell / Pascal / Volta)'
takes.take: Primary source on the hardware-compatibility break. Confirms Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta GPU support is now gone from official wheels.

takes.source: PyTorch dev-discuss — 'Python 3.10 support is being removed from PyTorch 2.15'
takes.take: Confirms 2.14 is the last release with Python 3.10 wheels; 2.15 requires Python 3.11+.
Primary documentation for the new one-sided transport API. Confirms the no-matching-receive semantics and that the API is experimental.

takes.source: FuturumGroup — 'PyTorch 2.15: Open-Source AI's Production Inflection Point'
takes.take: Enterprise-reliability framing of the release. Good for the broader context that 2.15 is the version where PyTorch moves from research-grade to production-grade distributed training.
